messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
I'm new to rocketry. Looking for about 750 ft. Landing under 6 m/s is a must. A single chute is fine. Plan for 12 mph wind. Something I can actually build, please.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 750 ft. 750 * 0.3048 = 229 m, so the band is roughly 217 to 240 m. Landing speed is a maximum of 6 m/s. Recovery is a single parachute (fixed). Wind is 12 mph: 12 * 0.447 = 5.36 m/s, and I will pass that on every flight. Rail length, launch angle and site altitude are not stated, so I use the 1.5 m rail, a vertical launch and sea level. Single stage, beginner materials (cardboard, balsa, a commercial Estes motor).
2. Feasibility: a drag-free coast to 229 m needs about sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 229) = 67 m/s at burnout. A 60 g model rocket throws away a large share of that to drag, so a B or a light C is the right class; a D would overshoot a first-build airframe. I need the catalog numbers before I pick.

2. Feasibility: the B6 is only 4.3 N*s and the catalog lists a single 0 s delay, so the chute would open at burnout and the rocket would never coast to 229 m. The B4 lookup returned 5.1 N*s but no ejection delays at all. The C6 is 8.8 N*s, average thrust 4.8 N, burn 1.83 s, and it has a 5 s delay. On a slim 25 mm tube that impulse usually clears 300 m; a standard BT-55 (about 34 mm) adds enough drag that 229 m is a fair first guess, and a beginner can buy the tube.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.075 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 4.8 / (0.075 * 9.81) = 6.52, above 3. Average acceleration on the rail is (4.8 - 0.736) / 0.075 = 54.2 m/s^2, so rail exit is about sqrt(2 * 54.2 * 1.5) = 12.8 m/s using average thrust. That sits under the 15 m/s gate, but the C6 spikes to 14.1 N, so the real exit speed should clear it. Descent mass is 0.075 - 0.011 = 0.064 kg. For 5 m/s at Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.064 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.0513 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.0513 / 3.1416) = 0.255 m. A 0.35 m plastic chute gives margin under 6 m/s. Burnout is at 1.83 s and a coast of a few seconds fits the 5 s delay.
4. Draft: 33.7 mm cardboard BT-55, 0.40 m long, 0.12 m hollow ogive nose, three 3.2 mm balsa fins, 18 mm mount and a C6-5. Single chute on motor ejection. Flying it in the stated 5.36 m/s wind.

4. Check: the simulator gives 254.4 m. Target is 229 m, and (254.4 - 229) / 229 = 0.111, so 11% high, outside the 5% band. That is the only miss. Rail exit 22.4 m/s clears 15 (my 12.8 m/s estimate ignored the thrust spike). Thrust-to-weight 7.4, margin 2.25 cal at rail exit and through the burn, landing 3.4 m/s under the 0.35 m chute. Liftoff mass is 0.0657 kg, lighter than the 0.075 kg guess, which is part of the overshoot. Ejection at 6.9 s is almost at apogee (6.69 s), so the 5 s delay is right.
5. Fix: apogee 254.4 m is high and the motor is already the smallest one with a useful delay, so I am increasing drag instead of adding clay. Drag area scales with diameter squared. 254.4 * (0.0337 / 0.036)^2 = 223 m, inside the band. Nose and body both go from 0.0337 m to 0.036 m. Fins, chute, motor and length stay put. The wider reference diameter should leave the margin near 2.25 * 0.0337 / 0.036 = 2.11 cal.

4. Check: the simulator gives 241.3 m. That is still high: (241.3 - 229) / 229 = 0.0537, about 5.4% over, just outside the 5% band. The diameter-squared guess of 223 m was too aggressive; the real drop was only 254.4 - 241.3 = 13.1 m. Everything else passes. Rail exit 21.4 m/s, thrust-to-weight 7.1, margin 2.02 cal, landing 3.5 m/s, chute out at 6.9 s against apogee at 6.56 s.
5. Fix: 241.3 m still misses the ceiling, so the same drag change goes one step further. The last 0.0023 m of diameter bought 13.1 m, and 241.3 - 229 = 12.3 m is still left, so nose and body go from 0.036 m to 0.038 m. Margin should stay near 2.02 * 0.036 / 0.038 = 1.91 cal. Nothing else changes.

4. Check: the simulator gives 230.9 m. Against 229 m that is (230.9 - 229) / 229 = 0.0083, under 1% and inside the 5% band. Rail exit 21.2 m/s is above 15, thrust-to-weight 6.9 is above 3, and the margin is 1.87 cal at rail exit and through the burn (my 1.91 cal guess was close). Landing is 3.6 m/s under the 6 m/s limit, with the chute out at 6.9 s, just after apogee at 6.49 s. Single C6, single chute.
5. Fix: no further change; every check passed.
6. Uncertainty: 230.9 m sits near the middle of the band, but OpenRocket's drag model and the real cardboard mass will move it. The airframe came out at 0.0711 kg; a lighter build climbs. In 5.36 m/s of wind the drift was 311 m, so this wants a large field even though no drift limit was set. Margin is 1.87 cal, enough to fly, and it will weathercock some.
messages.content:
A first-build cardboard rocket, 38 mm across and 0.52 m long, on an Estes C6-5 with one 0.35 m chute.
In a 5.36 m/s wind the simulator gives 231 m apogee, 21.2 m/s off the 1.5 m rail, and a 3.6 m/s landing.
